Choosing equipment is a fundamental early decision in apiculture, balancing design trade-offs and standardized dimensions [SRC-7f9fb3402aa7].

* **Hive Designs**: The Langstroth hive is the dominant design globally, built around removable vertical frames spaced with a precise "bee space" (roughly 6-9 mm) [SRC-7f9fb3402aa7].
This spacing prevents bees from building comb across gaps or sealing them entirely with propolis, allowing individual frames to lift out cleanly [SRC-7f9fb3402aa7].

* **Bottom Board**: Serves as the hive floor and features an entrance for the bees [SRC-7f9fb3402aa7].
* **Brood Boxes**: The lowest boxes where the queen lays eggs and the brood nest is maintained, typically reserved as the colony's unharvested space [SRC-7f9fb3402aa7].
* **Queen Excluder (Optional)**: A mesh grid featuring openings too small for the queen to pass through, keeping her restricted from honey supers so brood does not mix with harvestable honey [SRC-7f9fb3402aa7].
* **Honey Supers**: Boxes stacked above the brood nest designated for surplus honey harvest [SRC-7f9fb3402aa7].
* **Inner and Outer Covers**: Top layers providing insulation, ventilation, and weatherproofing [SRC-7f9fb3402aa7].
* **Frames and Foundation**: Each box contains standardized wooden or plastic frames holding foundation sheets embossed with hexagonal patterns for bees to draw out comb [SRC-7f9fb3402aa7].

Honey Bee Diseases and Pests in the UK – Overview for Beekeepers
Last updated: 15 August 2026
Honey bee diseases and pests are an unavoidable part of beekeeping, but with regular inspections, good hive hygiene and clear guidance they can be managed. This page provides an overview of the main disease and pest groups that affect colonies in the UK and explains how they link to day-to-day management, seasonal decision-making and the wider year in the apiary .
Disease prevention works best when combined with regular hive inspections , effective varroa management , good hive hygiene and an understanding of common hive problems that may initially resemble disease.
New beekeepers are often worried about getting everything wrong or missing early signs of trouble. The aim here is not to make you anxious, but to show that honey bee health is something you can monitor and improve over time, especially when you work alongside your local association, inspectors and official resources such as BeeBase. If you are not sure what problem you are looking at, try the interactive colony health triage tool to work through symptoms step by step, or use the bee health checker if you prefer a quicker symptom-based route. If the signs do not obviously fit foulbrood, varroa or a classic pest problem, the other conditions page is a useful next stop.
Quick triage: Not sure what you're seeing?
Use the interactive colony health triage tool
if you want a guided step-by-step route, or the Bee Health Checker
if you prefer a symptom-to-action table.
Download printable checker (Word/PDF)
Bee health also changes through the season. Spring inspections often focus on brood health, colony build-up and early warning signs, while late summer and early autumn are key periods for varroa control and winter preparation. For the bigger seasonal picture, see the year in the apiary , especially spring disease checks in April , May colony checks , late-summer varroa planning in August and September follow-up checks .
Common Bee Health Symptoms and Colony Problems
If you are looking for a specific symptom rather than a named disease, start here. These guides help you work from what you can see at the hive towards the most likely causes.
Main Categories of Honey Bee Diseases and Pests
Most honey bee health problems in the UK fall into a few broad groups. Understanding those groups makes it easier to narrow down likely causes when something does not look right in the hive.
Bacterial diseases include American foulbrood (AFB) and European foulbrood (EFB). These diseases affect developing brood and are taken very seriously in the UK because they are notifiable. Suspicious brood patterns, discoloured larvae, sunken cappings and unusual smells should never be ignored. The bacterial diseases guide explains the warning signs and links to the dedicated AFB and EFB pages.

This hub brings together everything you need for beginner beekeeping UK , keeping bees in the UK, hive inspections, hive management, swarm control, varroa, honey bee health, honey extraction and seasonal beekeeping advice.

Whether you are learning how to start beekeeping or building experience as a hobbyist beekeeper, these guides focus on real UK conditions — including unpredictable weather, short nectar flows, seasonal colony behaviour and practical apiary management — so you can make confident decisions throughout the beekeeping year.

Beekeeping can feel overwhelming at first. There is a lot to learn, plenty of opinions, and no shortage of advice that assumes perfect weather and endless forage. BeezKnees exists to make beekeeping in the UK clearer, calmer, and more practical — whether you are preparing for your first hive or refining your routine as a hobbyist beekeeper.

The UK beekeeping season brings its own challenges: unpredictable springs, short nectar flows, long wet spells, and sudden changes in colony behaviour. Success usually comes down to understanding the rhythm of the year, carrying out simple inspections well, and knowing what matters most at each stage.

Our beekeeping equipment guide for UK beginners explains what is essential, what can wait, and how to build your kit sensibly over time.

Course outline
Choosing equipment is the first concrete decision a new beekeeper makes, and it's worth understanding the trade-offs rather than just buying whatever a local supplier stocks.
Hive designs
Langstroth hives are the dominant design in North America and much of the world. They're built around removable vertical frames spaced with a precise "bee space" (roughly 6-9 mm) — a gap small enough that bees won't build comb across it, but large enough that they won't seal it with propolis. That spacing, patented by L.L. Langstroth in 1852, is what makes modern beekeeping practical: frames lift out individually for inspection without destroying comb, boxes stack to expand as the colony grows, and equipment is broadly standardized between suppliers and even between countries.
A Langstroth hive is built from stacked boxes ("supers"), from bottom to top:
Bottom board — the hive's floor, with an entrance for bees.
Brood box(es) — the lowest box(es), where the queen lays and the colony's brood nest lives; usually left as the colony's own, unharvested space.
Queen excluder (optional) — a mesh grid with openings too small for the queen to pass, keeping her out of honey supers so no brood ends up mixed with harvestable honey.
Honey supers — boxes added above the brood nest specifically for the colony's surplus honey, which is what a keeper harvests.
Inner cover and outer (telescoping) cover — top layers providing insulation, ventilation, and weatherproofing.
Each box holds a set of standardized frames — thin wooden or plastic rectangles that hold foundation (a thin sheet, often wax or plastic, embossed with a hexagonal pattern) on which bees draw out comb.
Top-bar hives (including the Kenyan and Tanzanian top-bar designs) take a different approach: a single long, usually horizontal box with individual wooden bars laid across the top, from which bees build their own comb downward with no foundation and no surrounding frame. They're cheaper and simpler to build, often preferred where standardized equipment is expensive to source, and some keepers consider the more "natural" comb-building beneficial. The trade-off is that top-bar comb is fragile, cannot be spun in a standard extractor, and isn't interchangeable with boxes from a different hive — each comb is unique to where it was built.
Horizontal hive designs
Both Langstroth and top-bar hives have horizontal variants that expand sideways along a single level rather than upward in stacked boxes — a real ergonomic consideration for a keeper who can't or doesn't want to lift a full deep box, which commonly weighs 36-45 kg (80-100 lb) once full of comb and honey (part of why many keepers deliberately use lighter medium or shallow boxes as honey supers instead, saving deeps for the brood nest):
Horizontal Langstroth hives ("long hives") use the same standardized Langstroth frames as a stacked vertical hive, just arranged side by side in one long box instead of stacked in boxes on top
